teacher_diagnoses.rule_anchor: Apply 11 U.S.C. § 522(d)(5) independently to any property, and retain it alongside every applicable specific paragraph.
Include Or. Rev. Stat. § 18.345(1)(p) as an independent general-personal-property alternative, even when a specific Oregon exemption also covers the asset.
Include 42 Pa. Cons. Stat. § 8123 as an independent general monetary exemption alongside any applicable specific Pennsylvania or federal exemption.

Include 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-1001(b) as an independent exemption for any other property, alongside a specific exemption such as wearing apparel, motor vehicle, or professionally prescribed health aid.
Do not treat jewelry as wearing apparel under § 33-1125(1).

Apply § 522(d)(5) independently to any property and retain it beside every qualifying specific paragraph. Its ceiling is $1,475 plus up to $13,950 of unused § 522(d)(1), so use $15,425 per debtor when no used homestead amount is supplied; for two equal joint debtors, the whole-asset ceiling is $30,850.

For the whole named asset, use the lesser of its value and $400,000 under § 33-1101(A), $15,000 under § 33-1123, $15,000 under § 33-1125(8), or $2,000 under § 33-1125(10). Apply § 33-1125(1) only to actual wearing apparel; jewelry qualifies only under a matching listed category, such as engagement or wedding rings under (4) or one watch under (6).
Include 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-1001(b) independently alongside any qualifying specific alternative.
Include Or. Rev. Stat. § 18.345(1)(p) independently alongside every applicable specific Oregon exemption. Its protected amount for the whole named asset is the lesser of the asset value and $400.

Include 42 Pa. Cons. Stat. § 8123 independently alongside every applicable specific Pennsylvania or federal exemption. Report the lesser of the whole asset value and $300 for one debtor; because each spouse receives the exemption, use a $600 whole-asset ceiling for two equal joint debtors.
Dollar ceilings limit protection but never defeat EC eligibility.

Include 42 Pa. Cons. Stat. § 8123 as an independent general monetary exemption alongside any applicable specific Pennsylvania or federal exemption. Its $300 amount is a protection ceiling, not an EC eligibility test.

Apply Wis. Stat. § 815.18(3)(d) to its listed consumer-goods categories, including household goods and furnishings, apparel, jewelry, books, musical instruments, firearms, sporting goods, and animals. Retain any independently applicable federal alternative.

For each citation use the smaller of the whole named asset's value and its ceiling: $27,900 for (d)(1), $4,450 for (d)(2), $700 for the named particular item under (d)(3), $1,875 for (d)(4), and $2,800 for (d)(6); (d)(9) has no stated ceiling.
A stated value above the statutory ceiling still permits the EC citation.

Then test the specific alternatives.
A pendant, necklace, bracelet, cocktail ring, or anniversary ring is not wearing apparel and does not qualify as an engagement or wedding ring without those facts.
Use the smaller of the whole asset value and $300 for one debtor or $600 for two equal joint debtors; determine which ceiling applies from the stated debtor count.

Use the substantive asset exemption: § 33-1101(A) for a qualifying occupied homestead, § 33-1123 for household furniture, goods, electronics, or appliances, § 33-1125(10) for firearms, and § 33-1125(8) for motor vehicles. A stated value above the statutory ceiling still permits the EC citation.

First add 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-1001(b) for every personal-use personal-property asset, including apparel, a vehicle, or a prescribed health aid; the words “any other property” do not make (b) mutually exclusive with a specific alternative.
A ceiling limits protection but never defeats EC eligibility.
Then independently add every matching specific Oregon category exemption.

For each citation use the smaller of the whole named asset's value and its ceiling: $27,900 for (d)(1), $4,450 for (d)(2), $700 for the named particular item under (d)(3), $1,875 for (d)(4), and $2,800 for (d)(6); (d)(9) has no stated ceiling.
Do not apply the § 12-1001 personal-property alternatives to property stated to be business-use.
Then test the specific alternatives.
Second add § 522(d)(5) to every asset without exception, including property already matching a specific paragraph.
Then independently add every matching specific Oregon category exemption.

Match § 815.18(3)(g) to a motor vehicle; when no used consumer-goods amount is supplied in this independent-pair task, its $4,000 vehicle amount plus unused (d) gives a $16,000 ceiling for one debtor or $32,000 for two equal joint debtors.

Use Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 33-1101(A) for an interest in the debtor's occupied dwelling, condominium, cooperative or qualifying mobile home; § 33-1123 for personally used household furniture, furnishings, household goods, consumer electronics or appliances not otherwise specifically prescribed; § 33-1125(8) for one motor vehicle; and § 33-1125(10) for firearms. Also apply the precise § 33-1125 numbered category when its described item is present, such as wedding rings, one watch, apparel, musical instruments, books, prescribed prostheses or household pets. A statutory dollar ceiling limits value protected and does not erase EC eligibility. Output the operative category citation, not headers or spouse-combination provisions.

For a jointly owned asset of two spouses, § 33-1121 permits combining the two personal-property exemptions, so sum their protected equal interests up to twice the applicable personal-property ceiling.

Also apply the precise § 33-1125 numbered category when its described item is present, such as wedding rings, one watch, apparel, musical instruments, books, prescribed prostheses or household pets.
